Mental health

Depression

More than sadness: symptoms, differences from grief, assessment, treatments and how to support someone.

Medical review Alejandro Rosàs, family doctor

Need help now? In Spain, 024 is free and open 24 hours; in an emergency call 112. Elsewhere, contact your local helpline or emergency services. This text is for general information: it cannot diagnose and does not replace seeing a professional. Where to get help →

What it is

Depression is a common disorder in which, for at least two weeks and for most of the day, there is a low mood or a loss of interest or pleasure, together with other symptoms:

  • changes in sleep (insomnia or oversleeping) and appetite;
  • tiredness and lack of energy;
  • difficulty concentrating or making decisions;
  • feelings of guilt or worthlessness;
  • slowing down or restlessness;
  • thoughts of death or suicide.

According to the World Health Organization it affects some 280 million people worldwide and is one of the leading causes of disability. It is more common in women and can appear at any age.

What it is not

Feeling sad after a loss or failure is human. Grief comes in waves, keeps moments of relief and usually centres on the person lost; depression tends to be more constant and to affect self-esteem. Sometimes both coincide. Depression is not laziness or weak character either, and it is not overcome just by "trying harder".

Some physical illnesses (underactive thyroid, anaemia, certain neurological diseases) and some medicines can cause similar symptoms.

How it is assessed

Through a clinical interview. Questionnaires such as the PHQ-9 help gauge severity. It is essential to ask directly about suicidal thoughts: asking does not cause them and makes it possible to help. Any past episodes of elation are also explored, because they would change the treatment (see bipolar disorder).

Which interventions are studied

  • Psychotherapy: cognitive behavioural therapy, behavioural activation, interpersonal therapy and brief psychodynamic therapies have proven efficacy, especially in mild and moderate cases.
  • Antidepressants: especially useful in moderate and severe depression. They take 2 to 6 weeks to work and should not be stopped abruptly.
  • Combining psychotherapy and medication usually gives better results in more severe cases.
  • Regular physical exercise, which has shown an effect on symptoms in trials, and keeping routines and social contact.
  • For severe or treatment-resistant depression there are other specialist options, such as electroconvulsive therapy, which is safe under anaesthesia and very effective in some cases.

How to seek help

Your family doctor is a good first step. If you have thoughts of ending your life, call 024 in Spain (free, 24 hours), your local crisis line, or emergency services if there is immediate danger.

How to support someone

  • Listen and validate ("I understand this is hard"), without judging or offering easy advice.
  • Suggest small, concrete activities: a walk, a meal together.
  • Encourage them to seek help and offer to go with them to the appointment.
  • If they mention death or suicide, take it seriously and ask directly.
  • Look after yourself too: supporting someone is draining.

Myths to avoid

  • "Antidepressants change your personality or are addictive". They are not addictive, though stopping them abruptly can cause withdrawal symptoms.
  • "People who talk about suicide don't do it". False: many people who die by suicide had told someone beforehand.
  • "Depression is just a lack of serotonin". It is an oversimplification: biological, psychological and social factors are involved.
